newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones to license DJIA for investments.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones to license DJIA for investments.

text.p: Dow Jones & Co. said Thursday it would license the Dow Jones industrial average, the world's most widely watched stock index, for investment products for the first time in the barometer's 101-year history.
Dow Jones said it licensed three exchanges to sell investment products based on the DJIA.
Dow said it expects DJIA products to begin trading some time in the fall and that it expects to award other DJIA licenses at a later date, but did not provide details.
Also, Dow did not rule out deals with its other indices, like the transports and utilities.
The Dow industrial average includes 30 blue-chip stocks and is widely viewed as a barometer of the U.S. stock market. Introduced in 1896, the average is the oldest continuing U.S. market index.
Dow said the deals would have a positive impact on financial results, but declined to be more specific.
"This is a historic event for Dow Jones & Co. and for investors everywhere," Chairman Peter Kann said.

"Once these products are registered, investors will be able to invest using the same tool they now use to follow the stock market -- the Dow Jones Industrial Average. This significantly reinforces Dow Jones' position as the premier provider of global market information."

Under the licensing deal, the American Stock Exchange will offer a unit investment trust, which is a variation of a mutual fund with a fixed, unmanaged stock portfolio that is liquidated after a specified time.
The Chicago Board of Trade will offer trading in futures contracts and options on futures contracts and the Chicago Board Options Exchange will offer trading in listed options contracts.
A Chicago Board of Trade spokesman said the exchange plans to open trading before the end of the year and analysts there said they expect retail customers to be attracted.

"It has an immediate kind of curb appeal for a retail investor because that's what they would know most about, the Dow," said Jim Collins, senior vice president for institutional financial futures at Smith Barney.

Anticipation of the product's success was reflected in the price of a membership that will allow trading in the DJIA futures contract. The price on the CBOT's IDEM seat, or Index Debt and Energy Market membership, rose Wednesday to $128,000 from $65,000.

A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell a commodity or financial instrument at a particular price on a certain date. An option is the right but not the obligation to buy or sell a commodity or financial instrument by a set date.
David Moran, president of Dow Jones Global Indexes, said the company decided that "increased sophistication" among investors fuelled the licensing deal.
Separately, Cramer Berkowitz & Co. said its president, James Cramer, sold most of the 1 million shares of Dow Jones & Co. that he controlled over the last few weeks.
Market sources said money manager Michael Price bought about 500,000 shares at $38 apiece. Cramer declined to comment.
In an interview, Price confirmed that he had recently increased his stake in Dow, and would be "patient" holding his position.
The Dow board is "very smart...and Peter Kann is a very good listener," he said. "The right decisions are going to get made. We think the (stock) value will go higher."
As of April, Price's Mutual Series mutual funds owned about 4.1 million of about 95 million Dow shares outstanding.

Cramer had tried to pressure Dow Jones to sell its electronic-information unit, Dow Jones Markets, formerly known as Telerate. Dow Jones announced in January plans to invest up to $650 million in coming years to strengthen the unit.
Dow Jones stock rose $1 to $40.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
